shippingNews.postTitle: Great Lakes-St. Lawrence Seaway Tonnage Up 3.5 Percent Through End of September

stories.body: Saltwater tanker transits the St. Lawrence Seaway. [Photo SLSMC] WELLAND CANAL – Nearly 25 million tonnes of cargo passed through the Great Lakes-St. Lawrence Seaway System by the end of September, up 3.5 per cent compared to the same time last year. It’s the second positive increase of the 2026 season, which began with March openings of the Welland Canal and Montreal-Lake Ontario sections of the 3,700-kilometre-long waterway. shippingNews.postTitle: Manistee Harbor Tours to Close Season with Fall Color Tours

stories.body: MANISTEE, MI – Manistee Harbor Tours will wrap up its 2026 sailing season with special fall color cruises aboard the Princess of Manistee this weekend and next weekend, offering passengers an opportunity to view the autumn scenery along Lake Michigan and the Manistee River. The two-hour cruises are scheduled from 2 to 4 p.m. Saturday and Sunday, Oct. 24-25, and again Oct. 31 and Nov. 1. These will be the final scheduled cruises of the year for the 65-foot passenger vessel. Capt. todayInHistory.title: Sam Laud
todayInHistory.text: Sam Laud Bay Shipbuilding Corp. of Sturgeon Bay, WI, laid the keel for their hull # 712 on Jan. 4, 1974 to be built as a smaller-sized Great Lakes self-unloading bulk cargo carrier. The new vessel was launched on Nov. 19, 1974 for Buffalo's American Steamship Co. (ASC), a subsidiary of GATX Corp., Chicago, IL. Completed in 1975, the self-unloader was christened Sam Laud by Mrs. Edna Laud on behalf of her husband at a christening ceremony held April 15, 1975. Mr. Laud was the former president (1945) and chairman of the board (1956) of GATX Corp., having started with the company in 1916 as shop painter and riveter. Mr. Laud died August 1, 1963. GATX Corp. had acquired ASC in July of 1973. Mrs. Laud was accompanied by Mr. Frederick G. Jaicks, chairman and CEO of Inland Steel Co., Chicago, IL, who gave the address at the christening ceremonies. One of a new generation of self-unloaders for the ASC fleet, the Sam Laud was built at an approximate cost of $13.3 million and was the fourth of 10 self-unloaders launched for the fleet under Chapter XI of the Merchant Marine Act of 1970. Under this act, the U.S. government-guaranteed financing and tax deferred benefits for fleet modernizing. The other ASC self-unloaders built under this program were the Roger M. Kyes (now Adam E. Cornelius, 1973), Charles E. Wilson (now John J. Boland, 1973), H. Lee White (1974), St. Clair (1976), Belle River (now Walter J. marineWeather.synopsis: High pressure builds to 30.6 inches over the Canadian Prairies today, pushing ridging of 30.4 inches over Lake Superior this evening. High pressure becomes centered over northern Ontario at 30.5 inches on Monday, shifting to the Saint Lawrence Seaway on Tuesday. A 29.7 inch low tracks from the northern Plains Tuesday night to the James Bay at 29.6 inches by Thursday morning, dragging a 29.9 inch trough across Lake Superior on Wednesday. High pressure of 30.2 to 30.3 inches returns to the Upper Great Lakes late Thursday into Friday.

Low pressure around 29.2 inches will move across Hudson Bay today, while high pressure around 30.6 inches will move from Alberta to the northern Great Lakes by Monday night. This will result in a slow moving cold front from north to south across Lake Michigan this afternoon through tonight. Thus modest southwest winds today will become north to northeasterly with the frontal passage. Breezy northeast winds will continue through Monday then southeasterly for Tuesday. Modest to breezy southerly winds will then prevail for the middle of the week.

The cold front has moved across western portions of Lake Superior this morning. This front slowly drops southeast across the region through Sunday night. Ahead of the front, southwest winds increase slightly on Sunday, with north winds filling in behind the front late Sunday into Monday. Following the passage of the cold front, a transient area of high pressure, averaging 30.60 inches, drops southeast across eastern Canada and the New England area through mid-week, while an area of low pressure lifts north across Northern Plains and up into the Canadian Prairies.

High pressure 30.50 inches along the East Coast will slide southwest today through the central Appalachians and into the Tennessee Valley. This will allow for a weak cold front to cross the lake on Monday. High pressure 30.50 inches will return on Tuesday and remain for much of the rest of the week.

A ridge averaging 30.5 inches affects the lake through tonight as the embedded high pressure center moves from near Lake Champlain toward the Mid-Atlantic states. The ridge then exits southeastward as a weak cold front sweeps southeastward across the lake on Monday. Behind the front, another ridge averaging 30.5 inches affects the lake through this Thursday as the embedded high pressure center wobbles southeastward from near Manitoba to North Atlantic waters southeast of the Canadian Maritimes.
